title: Gases and Atmospheric Chemistry
seo_title: Grade 11 Chemistry (SCH3U): Gases and Atmospheric Chemistry Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: The kinetic molecular theory; Boyle's, Charles's, Gay-Lussac's and the combined gas laws; the ideal gas law; molar volume at STP and SATP; gas stoichiometry; and the composition and pollution of the atmosphere. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Chemistry, Grade 11, University Preparation (SCH3U), Strand F: Gases and Atmospheric Chemistry)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Chemistry (SCH3U) worksheets on gases: the kinetic molecular theory, Boyle's and Charles's laws, the combined and ideal gas laws, molar volume at STP and SATP, and air quality. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Use kelvin in every gas law: T(K) = T(°C) + 273.
body_html:
How to think about it

Gas particles move fast and randomly, and their pressure comes from collisions with the walls. At constant temperature, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (Boyle). At constant pressure, V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ (Charles). Together, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.

The ideal gas law PV = nRT links pressure (kPa), volume (L), moles and kelvin temperature. One mole of any gas fills 22.4 L at STP (0 °C, 101.325 kPa) and 24.8 L at SATP (25 °C, 100 kPa).

Example

A gas at 100 kPa fills 6.0 L. It is squeezed to 2.0 L at the same temperature. New pressure?

P₂ = 100 × 6.0 ÷ 2.0

Answer: 300 kPa

Example

Volume of 2.00 mol of oxygen at STP?

V = 2.00 × 22.4

Answer: 44.8 L

Common mistakes

  • Using °C instead of kelvin in a gas law.
  • Mixing up STP (22.4 L/mol) and SATP (24.8 L/mol).
  • Thinking heavier gas molecules always take up more space: equal moles of any gas fill equal volumes.

faq.a: The gas particles slow down and hit the walls less hard, so the volume decreases at the same pressure.

A bicycle pump's outlet is blocked and the piston is pushed in slowly (constant temperature). What happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.e: The same particles are in a smaller volume, so they hit the walls more often.

items.q: A sealed syringe of air is put in a fridge. What happens to the pressure of the gas?

items.q: Why does a solid have a fixed shape?
c: Strong forces hold its particles in fixed positions.
Its particles do not move at all.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: A sealed can of gas is heated. What happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.e: The particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often and with more force.

items.q: A sealed balloon of air is left in the hot sun. Why does the pressure increase?
c: The particles hit each other more often, not the walls.
The mass of each particle changes.
The particles gain kinetic energy and hit the walls harder and more often, and the balloon expands.
items.e: Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls of the container.

items.q: Why is a gas easy to compress?

items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.
